list.listitem: Puberty is the period of human development during which sexual maturation occurs. C
Puberty is regulated by the hypothalamic-pituitary gonadal (HPG) axis, which directs the production of testosterone and estrogens. C
Most patients with pubertal delay have constitutional delay and progress normally into puberty without intervention. C
Reassurance and repeat physical exam with serum estradiol or testosterone level is appropriate when constitutional delay in growth and adolescence is suspected. C
Short courses of testosterone or estradiol may be considered in selected patients. B

Evaluation of other causes of pubertal delay begins with a careful history and physical exam, and serum levels of gonadotropins and testosterone or estradiol. Pubertal delay may be the first sign of a serious, life-threatening disorder. C

background.definition: Puberty is a process of developmental change that leads to secondary sexual development, growth, and fertility.

list.listitem: By definition, roughly 0.6% of children that fall more than 2.5 standard deviations above the mean may be labeled as having pubertal delay.
Constitutional delay is the most common cause of pubertal delay. In one study, 63% of males and 30% of females with pubertal delay had constitutional delay.
Etiologies of pubertal delay include constitutional delay, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, and hypergonadotropic hypogonadism. See "Differential Diagnosis" for details.
The primary risk factor is family history of pubertal delay.

Pulses of gonadotropin releasing hormone (GnRH) are released from the GnRH pulse generator in the hypothalamus in increasing amounts in early puberty, causing increased secretion of follicle stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH) from the anterior pituitary gland. This process is tightly regulated by intrinsic and extrinsic factors, including nutrition.

The pulse generator is also active during fetal development and in early infancy. The transient neonatal gonadotropin surge, referred to as "minipuberty," is thought to have a role in penile growth, testicular development, and language development. Once minipuberty is complete, the pulse generator is suppressed until the onset of puberty.
Increased FSH and LH secretion during puberty results in increased gonadal steroid secretion (either estrogen or testosterone) from the ovaries or testes.
Gonadal steroid secretion leads to the development of secondary sexual characteristics, changes in body composition, and increased growth velocity.
Adrenarche, the onset of adrenal steroid production by the adrenal gland, is controlled separately. Adrenarche leads to the development of axillary hair, pubic hair, body odor, and acne.
Pubertal status should be assessed annually using standardized physical exam criteria as a part of the health supervision visit. C
Annual health supervision visits that include assessment of pubertal status are recommended by the American Academy of Pediatrics.

Boys normally begin puberty between 9 and 14 years. In girls, pubertal development begins between ages 8 and 13 years according to normative data, but the age of onset appears to be decreasing, and there are ethnic differences in pubertal timing. Timing of pubertal onset can be affected by obesity, with earlier pubertal onset often seen in overweight and obese girls.
Pubertal development is assessed by physical exam using standard criteria (Tanner stages or sexual maturity rating stages ).
Evaluation of breast development in females and genitalia development in males allows assessment of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis.
Evaluation of pubic hair development in both sexes allows assessment of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis.
While there is often correlation between breast/genitalia and pubic hair development, they are best assessed separately.
Pubertal development should begin by the age of 13 years in girls and the age of 14 years in boys and should progress at an appropriate rate. C

Laboratory diagnosis of pubertal delay begins with establishing levels of gonadotropins (FSH and LH) and testosterone or estradiol. Markedly elevated levels of LH and FSH indicate gonadal failure, while normal or low levels indicate gonadotropin deficiency or constitutional delay. C

list.listitem: If pubertal delay is suspected, a history of excessive exercise, symptoms of chronic disease, and family history of pubertal delay should be elicited. Review of systems should include screening for intracranial lesions. A history of developmental delay may imply a CNS defect associated with gonadotropin deficiency.
Dysmorphic features should be noted as they may correlate with a genetic syndrome known to be associated with pubertal delay.
Height percentiles and growth velocity should be measured.
In females, increased growth velocity is the first sign of puberty, though breast development is what will be noticed on exam. In males, testicular enlargement is the first sign of puberty.

Physical exam will show Tanner 1 pubertal development if puberty has not yet begun. In boys, this corresponds to <4 mL in testicular volume or <2.5 cm of testicular length in the long axis. In girls, this corresponds to an absence of glandular breast tissue.
See chapter on precocious puberty for recommended history and physical examination for precocious puberty.

For delayed puberty, order serum gonadotropins (LH and FSH), testosterone (boys), and estradiol (girls). Testosterone and estradiol must be obtained by high sensitivity pediatric assay (HPLC tandem mass spectrometry) for results to be meaningful. LH and FSH should be measured via highly sensitive immunometric assay. These specialized assays typically require a national send-out laboratory. Pediatric standards must be used to interpret results.

FSH and LH will help differentiate gonadal failure from constitutional delay or hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. In the case of gonadal failure, FSH and LH will be markedly elevated. Serum LH in the pubertal range suggests that puberty is progressing and supports a diagnosis of constitutional delay.

A bone age is indicated in patients with pubertal delay who have normal or low gonadotropins. Delayed bone age (typically greater than 2 SD from the mean) is seen in patients with constitutional delay.
Obtaining a karyotype is indicated when there is a suspicion of a chromosomal abnormality such as Klinefelter syndrome or Turner syndrome.

Thyroid testing may in rare instances uncover hypothyroidism as a cause of pubertal delay. Testing for hypothyroidism is necessary if additional symptoms are present (dry skin, constipation, cold intolerance, etc.).
Multiple endocrine deficiencies or CNS symptoms should prompt brain MRI scanning for CNS tumors or congenital defects.
Additional workup will be guided by history and physical exam (e.g. laboratory screening for celiac disease or inflammatory bowel disease).
See chapter on precocious puberty for diagnostic testing of precocious puberty.
Patients should be evaluated for pubertal delay when secondary sexual development does not begin by the age of 13 in girls or by the age of 14 in boys (see ).

Patients who do not progress normally through puberty should also be evaluated. Girls should be menarchal within 5 years of breast bud development and boys should reach Tanner stage 5 pubertal development within 4.5 years of pubertal onset. Patients who stall in pubertal development are not likely to have constitutional delay.

See chapter on precocious puberty for approach to patient with early puberty (girls with breast development before 7 years if Caucasian and 6 years if African American and boys with testicular enlargement before 9 years).
Reassurance and repeat physical exam with serum estradiol or testosterone level is appropriate when constitutional delay in growth and adolescence is suspected. C
Short courses of testosterone or estradiol may lead to initiation of puberty in patients with constitutional delay who are particularly distressed about their condition. B
Long-term hormonal replacement is indicated for patients with permanent forms of hypogonadism to induce and maintain secondary sexual characteristics and promote skeletal health. C

Short-term hormonal treatment with gonadal steroids (testosterone or estradiol) will increase growth velocity and elicit secondary sexual development in patients with constitutional delay of puberty. Testosterone treatment can be repeated once if there is no physical or laboratory effect following a 4- to 6-month period of no therapy. Long-term therapy is not indicated since it will lead to epiphyseal fusion and shorter adult height. This treatment should not begin in boys before a bone age of 12 years (or chronological age of 14 years) and should not begin in girls before a bone age of 11-12 years (or chronological age of 13 years).
Permanent hypogonadism is treated with replacement therapy of testosterone or estradiol. Doses are gradually increased over time to mimic normal puberty.
Calcium supplementation should be encouraged for bone health, although there are no long-term data to support the efficacy of this treatment.
See chapter on precocious puberty for drug therapy of advanced pubertal development.
In rare cases, pubertal delay is caused by CNS tumors, which interfere with hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal function. Surgical resection is indicated in many of these cases.
Psychological support is indicated for some patients with pubertal delay since they may experience poor self-esteem and body image.
Males report a higher frequency of psychosocial problems than females.
Patients with pubertal delay should be referred to a pediatric endocrinologist, unless it is clear to the examiner that the patient has constitutional delay.
Patients with CNS tumors should additionally be referred to a pediatric oncologist and neurosurgeon.
Untreated permanent hypogonadism can lead to decreased bone density, decreased muscle mass, and failure of development of secondary sexual characteristics.
Testosterone therapy can cause side effects, including increased cholesterol levels, priapism, headache, and injection site reactions.
Estrogen therapy can cause side effects, including thrombosis, nausea and vomiting, mood changes, and dry eyes.
Most patients with pubertal delay have constitutional delay and progress normally into puberty without intervention. C
Without treatment, hypogonadal patients will not develop and maintain secondary sexual characteristics and are at high risk for osteoporosis. B
Typical course depends on underlying etiology.
Most patients with pubertal delay have constitutional delay and will progress normally into puberty without intervention.
Untreated hypogonadal patients are at risk of osteoporosis as gonadal steroids are critical for bone mineralization.
Short stature, failure to develop secondary sexual characteristics, and infertility are typical in untreated patients.
Prognosis of precocious puberty is discussed separately.
When treated, patients with hypogonadism will develop secondary sexual characteristics and have increased bone mass.
Fertility may be achieved, depending on the underlying diagnosis.
An earlier age at menarche is associated with increased depressive symptoms in adolescence, based on a Norwegian Mendelian randomization study.

Serial physical exams for monitoring of pubertal development and repeat laboratory testing to establish onset of rising levels of sex steroids are indicated. If pubertal development fails to occur by the age of 18 years, gonadotropin deficiency is usually the diagnosis.
Females on replacement estrogen therapy should have yearly gynecologic exams.
